title: John Filson / Kentucke 1784
summary: Pennsylvania schoolteacher and surveyor John Filson reached Lexington around 1783 with land warrants for more than 12,000 acres. In 1784 he published The Discovery, Settlement…
bodyMarkdown:
John Filson (c. 1747 – 1788) was a schoolteacher and surveyor who wrote the first book-length history of Kentucky, published with a map in 1784. The book and map drew settlers west and made Daniel Boone famous. It also spread a picture of Kentucky that served settlers' claims at the expense of Native nations.

## From Pennsylvania to Kentucky

The [Wikipedia biography of John Filson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Filson) says he was born in Chester County, Pennsylvania, around 1747. A John Filson served as an ensign in a Pennsylvania battalion and was taken prisoner at Fort Washington in November 1776. Filson worked as a schoolteacher and surveyor in Pennsylvania until 1782 or 1783.

He then acquired western land and moved to Kentucky, but sources differ on how much. Wikipedia says over 13,000 acres. The [Filson Historical Society's timeline entry](https://filsonhistorical.org/cool_timeline/john-filson-publishes-the-discovery-settlement-and-present-state-of-kentucke/) says 12,000 acres, and that he arrived in 1783.

## Kentucke

Filson wrote The Discovery, Settlement and Present State of Kentucke while in Kentucky. In the summer of 1784 he went to Wilmington, Delaware, to have it published. The map was printed in Philadelphia. According to Wikipedia, the edition of book and map ran to 1,500 copies priced at $1.50.

A French edition appeared in Paris in 1785 and a German one in Leipzig in 1790.

The book contained what the Filson Historical Society calls the first biographical information, lore and legend of Daniel Boone, whom Filson met and interviewed.

## The "Dark and Bloody Ground"

The Filson Historical Society notes that the book widely circulated the myth of Kentucky as a "Dark and Bloody Ground." That image benefited colonial settlers' claims to the land and encouraged European settlement.

## Losantiville

After several years in Kentucky teaching, surveying and fighting lawsuits, Filson bought a one-third interest from Mathias Denman in a tract on the Ohio opposite the mouth of the Licking River. Wikipedia gives its size as 800 acres. The [Grokipedia entry on Cincinnati](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cincinnati) says Denman, Israel Ludlow and Robert Patterson acquired about 740 acres.

The sources also disagree on who named the town. Wikipedia says Filson coined Losantiville from Latin, Greek and French words meaning "the town opposite the mouth." Grokipedia says Ludlow coined it. Grokipedia dates the founding to December 28, 1788. In 1790 territorial governor Arthur St. Clair renamed the town Cincinnati.

## Disappearance

Filson never saw the town grow. On October 1, 1788, during a surveying trip near the Great Miami River, his party was attacked by Shawnees, and he disappeared. His body was never found. His partners transferred his interest to Israel Ludlow, and his heirs never benefited from the land.

## Kentucky today

Filson's name lives on in the Filson Historical Society, whose timeline calls him Kentucky's first well documented historian. The same entry notes that the book helped spread the "Dark and Bloody Ground" myth.
